title: Rav Ilish
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Hyman recounts: In Gittin 45, it is told that Rav Ilish saw a wondrous thing about the daughters of Rav Nachman, who were stirring in a pot with their hands (and their hands were not burned). He said: It is written, "but a woman among all these I have not found" — yet here are the daughters of Rav Nachman. It happened that Rav Ilish was taken captive, and the daughters of Rav Nachman were also taken captive and brought to one place. One day a moment of opportunity arrived when he could flee. He said: Let me go and see the daughters of Rav Nachman, and if they are truly righteous a miracle will happen for all of us. He overheard them saying to one another: What do we lack here? In Nehardea we had husbands, and here too we will not lack; let us tell the captors to take us to a distant place so that our husbands will not come to ransom us. And he fled and was saved, and then understood that they had done this by means of sorcery.

And as it appears to Hyman, he was one of the judges of the city of Mechoza under Rava. In Bava Batra 133b: Rav Ilish thought to speak before Rava — Rava said to him: Do judges of compromise [דחצצתא] rule like this? — Rav Ilish was ashamed. Rava applied to him the verse "I the Lord will hasten it in its time." And in Gittin 77b he raised a difficulty against Rava (concerning the principle) that what a wife acquires, her husband acquires — Rava was ashamed.

Hyman writes: He is likewise mentioned in Pesachim 65b. And he died during Rava's lifetime, in Bava Metzia 68b [printed כב״מ; supplied transcription כב״ב], where they said: Against the sons of Rav Ilish a certain document emerged — Rava said: Rav Ilish was a great man, and he would not have caused people to consume something prohibited.

notes.text: Hyman describes the daughters stirring with their hands, then later reports Ilish’s sorcery conclusion. Rav Nachman’s full name supplies the repeated RN.

The Chatzatzta judge phrase remains a precise lexical/place-form question; Hyman’s apparently inference about judges of Mechoza is not established by name harmonization. His final statement means not causing others to consume something prohibited.

The saved William Davidson Bava Batra133b paragraph contains דייני דחצצתא. Its named English translation at133b:2 interprets the phrase as judges of compromise. The body adopts that local lexical interpretation, with the Hebrew word displayed; it does not establish a town or prove an office held by Ilish. As it appears to Hyman preserves the tentative force of וכפי הנראה: the proposed Mechoza judgeship remains Hyman’s inference and the p003 source hold remains. Ilish’s embarrassment in this exchange and Rava’s embarrassment in the separate Gittin account remain distinct. The selected paragraph does not independently establish the other narrative, death chronology or supplied folio references. Those source claims and inherited English remain without a new historical admission. Both existing mixed notes remain verbatim, including their earlier lexical question and prohibition explanation; no mixed note is retired. Earlier English questions and all source spellings remain archived. No additional legal details, primary-text figures, authority binding or printed correction-history claim are imported.

The whole consulted Gittin 45a story includes the birds, Ilish’s own miraculous escape and the later return of Rav Nachman’s daughters before his sorcery conclusion. Hyman’s abridged narration and its wording about a miracle for all are retained without inserting the omitted story. In Bava Batra 133b, Ilish is embarrassed and Rava applies the verse to him; in Gittin 77b, Rava is embarrassed by Ilish’s question, followed by further discussion. The two roles are not reversed. The named Davidson interpretation of דחצצתא as judges of compromise does not independently establish Hyman’s tentative Mechoza office inference. The printed Hyman notice, III p.981, actually cites כב״מ סח:, Bava Metzia 68b, for the document concerning Ilish’s sons; the supplied transcription has כב״ב, Bava Batra. The whole matching Bava Metzia paragraph continues onto 69a. That printed-versus-transcribed reference difference is disclosed in the English while the supplied Hebrew remains unchanged. Hyman’s inference that Ilish died during Rava’s lifetime remains his historical conclusion; the consulted English also describes the sons’ document as their late father’s venture. Pesachim 65b directly names Ilish in the Paschal-lamb carrying remark, without establishing a universal namesake identity.
